items.headline: Foundry's SmartRoto: AI-assisted roto that aims to work the way you do
items.body_text:
Foundry has released SmartRoto, a new AI-powered plugin for Nuke, NukeX, Nuke Studio and Nuke Indie that aims to take the grind out of one of the most tedious jobs in visual effects: rotoscoping. We spoke to Adam Cherbetji, Foundry’s Director of Product for AI Research, ahead of the launch.

The first thing to understand about SmartRoto is what it is not. It is not a magic bullet, and it is not another automated matting tool that draws a spline around a segmentation mask. “This isn’t the magic bullet, it doesn’t do the full spline creation for you, it’s about accelerating the keyframing process,” Cherbetji told us. “There is so much artist intuition that goes into the breakdown of the subject into the smaller shapes. And whilst that is somewhat time-consuming, – the really time-consuming part is then the keyframing, …so that’s where we focused.”

In other words, the artist still does what good roto artists have always done: break the subject down into sensible, articulated shapes on a frame where everything is clearly visible. SmartRoto then takes over the part of the job nobody enjoys, moving, animating and deforming those splines across the image sequence to follow the subject.

SmartRoto annual subscriptions are priced at US$499/year, with node-locked and floating licenses available.

Smart keys and user keys

The workflow is built around a distinction between two kinds of keyframes. Keys the model predicts are called ‘smart keys’. Keys the artist places or corrects are user keys, and these are treated as gospel. “If you’ve positioned it there, we take it as gospel that we’re not going to change it,” Cherbetji explained.

In practice, you create your shapes on a clean frame, then key another significant frame, much as you would working manually. Then hit a key and SmartRoto snaps your roto shapes into place. If the prediction is slightly off, you adjust it, which promotes that frame to a new locked user key. Then you run the model again and it fills in the gaps, either across the whole sequence or just a subsection you are working through.

Critically, corrections feed back into the system. If the middle of an arc is a bit off, you fix that frame, it becomes a user key, and re-running the model takes your updated information into account across the surrounding range. You are giving the model direction, not fighting it. There is no scenario, therefore, where you are presented with a result so wrong you have to start over; the fix is always just an adjustment, never a full redo.

The model does produce a dense set of keyframes, which traditionally would be undesirable since dense keys are painful to manipulate. But because only user keys ever need your attention, the density does not get in your way. The Foundry has included a thinning tool that analyses the motion between keys and looks for ranges that can be represented with interpolation. Cherbetji was candid that this is an area the team wants to keep developing.

User keys vs predicted smart keys

It is worth digging a little deeper into this two-tier keyframe system, because it is the heart of how SmartRoto stays on the artist’s side. At one point in development, the user keys were called ‘gold keys’ as they are the real anchor points. The distinction is simple but powerful: user keys are treated as a source of truth and are used to guide the prediction of the smart keys. User keys will never be overwritten. And the granularity is per shape, not per frame — on any given frame it is possible to have a mixture of some shapes with user keys and some with smart keys, so you can lock down the shapes you are happy with while the model keeps refining the rest.

Foundry’s suggested workflow runs like this:

Create roto shapes on the initial frame, choose a frame where your subject is fully in frame and unoccluded.

Jump ahead and create a keyframe, choose a frame where there are significant changes to the subject. Select a group of shapes and create a smart key using the roto current frame button.

Review and adjust: make sure the created smart key properly aligns with the subject, tweaking the shape or hitting the Convert Current Smart Key button to lock it in.

Repeat: depending on the complexity of the shot, you may need to create a few keyframes to help guide the model.

Set the working range: configure the working range in the properties, whether input, custom or in/out points. This sets the bounds when SmartRoto runs across the sequence.

SmartRoto the sequence: the Create Smart Keys controls track the shapes across the working range.

Review and adjust: if there are frames SmartRoto hasn’t got quite right, make adjustments to those frames, creating new user keys to guide SmartRoto, and repeat the process.

Iterate to perfection.

If that reads like a description of how a good roto artist already works, establish the extremes, refine the in-betweens, lock …what’s right, – that is exactly the point.

Not optical flow, not segmentation

We asked how the system works in principle. Cherbetji was clear it is neither of the two obvious candidates. “Not optical flow, that’s been tried. It was the first thing we attempted. Optical flow breaks down at the edge. That’s exactly where you need the precision.” Nor is it image-based matting. “A lot of the solutions we’ve seen in the market so far are using a segmentation model and drawing a spline around that. We don’t think that’s fit for purpose either.”

Instead, the machine learning model latches onto image features and propagates the splines themselves. This matters because splines remain the currency of roto, and they are subpixel-accurate. If one was to constrain them to what is merely easily visible in a matte, you’d throw precision away.

items.headline: Great ways to use Auto Mask in Final Cut Pro
items.body_text:
The big three editing apps (Final Cut Pro, Premiere, Resolve) all copy features from one another, sooner or later. Sometimes this doesn’t take long (FCP’s Voice Isolation was copied by Resolve, Resolve’s curves were copied by FCP and Premiere) while sometimes it takes over a decade (Premiere’s timeline now displays a ripple operation similar to the new FCP rather than the classic FCP).

Resolve’s Magic Mask inspired FCP’s (faster) Magnetic Mask and eventually Premiere’s Object Mask, and these similar features are very useful in all these apps. Auto Mask is, for now at least, only in FCP, and it’s stunningly good. It’s not tracking, and in many cases, it’s a better solution.

Instead of tracking an item, person, object or anything else through a shot, it simply recognizes people, or parts of people, parts of a scene, or even pets, live on every frame. This approach is remarkably resistant to occlusion, making it a practical way to perform selective color correction and lots more besides.

Though I covered a few ideas in my initial article on FCP 12.3, it’s worth a second look. Let’s start with an overview before getting into the weeds.

Auto Mask basics

There are two simple ways to begin.

To use Auto Mask to control visibility of a clip, add the Auto Mask effect (in the Masks and Keying category) directly to a clip.

To use Auto Mask to restrict an effect or color correction, click the new Auto Mask button that’s visible in every effect header. (Shape Masks and Color Masks are now also available here.)

In the Auto Mask menu, you can now choose what to reveal — here’s the full list or 17 possible masks:

Person

People

Skin

Skin and Face

Hair

Facial Hair

Mouth

Lips

Teeth

Eye

Eyebrow

Clothing

Scene

Sky

Foliage

Foreground

Background

Animals

Dog

Cat

Each Auto Mask can be added, subtracted or intersected with others, so you could select, for example, animals in the foreground that aren’t cats. Shrink/Expand, Erode and Blur can also be adjusted for fine-tuning.

When applied to color corrections, you’ll have the standard Inside/Outside switch, to let you easily access change both sides of the mask, but if you need to, you can invert a mask using the menu to the right of an effect header.

The Magnetic Mask, Color Mask and Shape Mask are all still here too, giving you many ways to amend an Auto Mask. This isn’t always necessary, but sometimes a shape won’t be recognized correctly on every frame, causing all or part of an object to flick in and out of the mask. Lips viewed from the side may not always be found, for example, and if a subject is wearing over-ear headphones, the gap between their head and the headphones may come and go.

Still, in most shots, Auto Mask is reliable, useful, and fast.

OK, basics sorted. Let’s get into some practical workflows for Auto Mask.

Correcting color parts of people

This is one of the most obvious uses, but also one of the most practical. While not all subjects are sensitive about their appearance in professional videos, many are, and Auto Mask opens up whole new categories of potential changes.

For example, a subject may not like how their lipstick shade appears on camera, and while changing it could have once been a tricky fix, it’s now pretty straightforward, because you can add Color Wheels, then apply an Auto Mask to Lips. Do check that the mask has been correctly detected on every frame, though.

Teeth can be easily whitened by a saturation reduction with exposure adjustments, and an Auto Mask set to Teeth. Eyebrows can be darkened or lightened too. Skin adjustments work well, so if a subject you film regularly wants to even out a changing tan across a series of videos, now you can. Clothing is straightforward to select, but as all clothes will be selected, you may need a further color, shape or magnetic mask to limit it.

Before you try to turn dark hair blonde, here’s the most important rule I learned during my time as a retoucher:

Retouching, like any lie, is easier to get away with if it’s close to the truth.

To put it another way, smaller changes usually look better than big ones.

There’s more to color than you may have considered, and changing hair color is not a simple hue or brightness shift. Color Wheels are a good place to start, as you’ll probably want to carefully consider how to push the shadows, midtones, and highlights in saturation and hue. A hue rotation can sometimes be helpful here too. If you need finer control, Curves is what you need.

For a great demo of what’s possible, check out Jenn Jager’s video:

Censoring mouths

This is a nice one if you need to cover up a mouth during outbursts of profanity, and it’s easy. Blade around the section you need to cover, then find the Stylize category of video effects, add the Pixellate effect to that section, and apply an Auto Mask set to Mouth. Adjust the size of the blocks, then Expand and Blur the mask to suit. To handle audio, add the Test Oscillator audio effect to the bladed section to replace it with a suitable beep.

For a video version of this tip and several more ideas, check out Brad West’s video here:

Colorizing black and white videos

By applying different color corrections to different parts of a person, it’s possible to restore color to a black and white image, one part at a time. You could even achieve a similar effect using a color image as your starting point, but you’d probably want to use the Tint effect rather than color corrections to achieve that flat-color look.

Robin Kurz’s video covers many other tips alongside this one:

Sky Replacements, simple and advanced

The easy one here is a simply color correction. Add a Color Wheels or something else, tweak some settings, add an Auto Mask set to Sky. This can make a light sky deeper or more vibrant, but to truly replace the sky you’ll need to add your own new sky.

images.cap: In the header of an effect, you choose Auto Mask from the new “person” icon

It’s not easy to find or make an image with all 17 masks, but if you can assemble some pets, a person with hair and a beard with their eyes and mouth open, near some plants and in front of some sky, you’ll get there
Correct both sides of a mask, or invert it
Color changes often work well — can you spot which is the original?
Oh no! I’ve been hit by the Paper Ray!
Something between live action and animation

items.headline: Foundry Launches Griptape Enterprise for Secure AI-Accelerated VFX Workflows
items.body_text:
Foundry has launched Griptape Enterprise, a new tier of its Griptape AI workflow orchestration platform designed to bring secure, professional-grade AI-accelerated workflows to high-end media production.

The update adds studio-controlled licensing and expanded project management capabilities, allowing pipeline supervisors to curate which models artists use so workflows remain vetted, compliant and production-ready. Studios can run Griptape Enterprise within on-premises or private cloud infrastructure, keeping sensitive IP, prompt inputs and private training data inside the facility.

Foundry also appointed Kyle Roche as chief AI officer to guide its next-generation technology development, including Foundry Research initiatives. Roche, Griptape co-founder and former CEO, joined Foundry in February 2026 following the company’s acquisition of the AI orchestration platform.

“Foundry has been a trusted technology partner to visual effects and animation studios for over 30 years,” Roche said. “With the new Griptape Enterprise license tier, Foundry is shepherding high-end creative teams into AI-enhanced production in a safe and secure way—with artistry and craft at its core. While studios are navigating how best to integrate AI models with bespoke platforms and workarounds, we’re pleased to offer Griptape as a highly customizable and safe off-the-shelf alternative.”

Built on a Python-based architecture, Griptape enables artists and studios to orchestrate multiple AI models and agents across the pipeline, from creative workflows to technical tasks such as data and metadata management. Griptape Enterprise adds studio governance, production-driven pipeline automation and commercially cleared infrastructure intended to meet security and legal compliance demands.

Key Enterprise tier features include:

Enterprise Governance and Infrastructure Control: Studios run Griptape on-premises within their network security perimeter, keeping sensitive IP, prompt inputs, and private training data inside the facility. Centrally managed unlimited licensing and permissions control how artists and automated workloads can access AI models and software features, keeping environments aligned with studio standards.

Key Griptape updates:

Studio-Grade Plate and Colour Management: Griptape understands image sequences the way industry-standard production tools like Nuke do, and Griptape’s OpenColorIO library brings color management in line with the rest of the pipeline.

Show-Ready Projects: Templates define project workspaces, libraries, versioning, and naming conventions. Library versions pin per show or per shot, so each production keeps its approved toolset and reopens reliably even as the pipeline moves on.

Nuke Integration: TDs build a workflow in Griptape, expose the controls artists need, and publish it into the pipeline as a versioned Nuke gizmo. Griptape workflows can also run Nuke scripts headlessly as part of a larger AI pipeline.

Agentic Automation: The built-in AI assistant accelerates artist work in Griptape, with the choice of local or cloud LLMs. MCP server lets AI agents pilot Griptape at scale, and AI coding skills, the same Foundry uses internally, let studios rapidly build their own trusted node libraries.

Modular Diffusion Pipelines: Griptape breaks image and video generation into stages that artists can rearrange, chain, and refine, rather than a single fixed generate step. Models like FLUX, Stable Diffusion XL, LTX, and WAN run locally on studio GPUs.

Griptape Enterprise is now available. More information including pricing can be found here.

Source: Foundry

items.headline: 'This Is a Black-and-White Issue': Jorge R. Gutierrez Says Death Threats Drove Decision to Axe His GenAI Animated Project at Amazon
items.body_text:
Speaking to Variety this week, celebrated animator Jorge R. Gutiérrez (The Book of Life, Maya and the Three) shared how anti-AI sentiment took an extreme turn after Amazon MGM/AWS announced his show Punky Duck as one of the titles greenlit from its new GenAI Creators’ Fund. In a headspinning turnaround, Gutiérrez shut down his own show within 36 hours of its announcement.

As it unfolded on his social media feeds, the project was announced on a Wednesday. By Thursday, he shared he was reconsidering based on reactions and “learning a lot from many of you.” And on Friday, he officially pulled the plug, writing in a post: “My intent was to showcase artists, both new and seasoned, both inside and outside the studios, driving this new tech. My sincerest apology to those I upset. I promise to do better moving forward. Thank you for your patience with me. I will try harder.”

Gutiérrez explained to Variety that the project’s announcement was swiftly followed by doxxing of his home address and death threats against himself and his wife, animator/artist Sandra Equihua, with whom he co-created the Nickelodeon series El Tigre: The Adventures of Manny Rivera. His intention was to entrench human creators within the GenAI animation landscape — “to make sure artists are guaranteed a seat at the table, […] make sure this [show] is driven by artists” — but artists and fans opposed to the use of GenAI had an immediate, virulent reaction to the news.

“What I quickly learned is this is a black-and-white issue. You’re pro or you’re anti — there’s no in between right now,” he told Variety. “The road to hell is paved with good intentions. My intentions were good, but I was taking my family to hell by doing this.” Amazon released Gutiérrez from the gig easily, saying he should do what was best for his family.

Gutiérrez is an Emmy and Annie Award-winning Mexican animator and director, known for El Tigre, his feature film directorial debut The Book of Life and his acclaimed Netflix event series Maya and the Three. His upcoming projects include original animated features I, Chihuahua (with Snafu Pictures) and La Venganza Rodríguez, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s Speedy Gonzalez movie, adult series concept El Guapo vs. the Narco Vampires, and 3Doubles’ Lovecraft-inspired anthology project, Ages of Madness.

Gutiérrez’s alarming personal experience is a pinpoint of the broader societal grappling over the ethics and value of GenAI. According to Google figures analyzed by AI pre-production platform Filmustage, searches related to damming the artificial intelligence tide in entertainment have been on the rise. The search phrase “stop AI in film” increased +37,157% year-on-year, “ban AI movies” was up +9,857%” and searches for “movies with no AI” were up +3,387%.

The debate is heated within the animation community, as studios and individual creators explore the technology’s production and design generation possibilities and human artists worry over the rise of a new threat to their jobs in an already challenging sector. Major studios have forged partnerships with GenAI tool developers and sued others for using their IP without permission, film festivals and exhibitors face backlash for platforming AI productions, whole studios built around AI pipelines emerge — indies and experimental outfits from established labels alike. GenAI is either the gateway to a liberating future for animation; simply the latest filmmaking evolution, like CGI, color or sound; or an apocalyptic plague on creativity, depending who you ask.

items.headline: Latest Dalet Flex LTS Boosts AI Workflows, Deepens Dalia Integration
items.body_text:
Dalet, a technology and service provider for media-rich organizations, announced the latest Long-Term Supported (LTS) release of Dalet Flex. Building on recent investments in usability, AI services and workflow modernization, the new release introduces intelligent automation across each stage of the media life cycle, from content acquisition and enrichment to editing, packaging and distribution, helping organizations produce and deliver more content with greater speed, efficiency and operational control.

Media organizations today face growing pressure to produce more content for more platforms with leaner teams and increasingly complex workflows. This Dalet Flex LTS release addresses these challenges by expanding AI-powered media intelligence through workflow automation and deeper integration with Dalia, Dalet’s media-aware agentic AI platform. Organizations can further streamline operations while operationalizing the next generation of intelligent media workflows.

“Dalet Flex is the operational backbone for modern media organizations,” says Erwan Kerfourn, head of product for Dalet Flex. “This release advances the level of intelligent capabilities customers can access across their workflows, enabling them to achieve greater efficiencies and new ways of working using Dalia as a practical part of their everyday media operations.”

The Dalet Flex LTS updates introduce significant enhancements that simplify content acquisition while improving security, operational visibility and workflow efficiency.

Support for OpenID Connect authentication strengthens enterprise security by enabling modern identity management and secure user authentication across Dalet Flex environments. New role-based permissions within Ingest Portal provide administrators with greater control over scheduling and recording operations while improving governance for distributed production teams.

At the same time, a modernized Ingest Portal makes distributed live production materially more efficient thanks to streamlined scheduling, multi-time-zone visibility, FIFO scheduling for Dalet Brio and broader format support, including DNxHD for the Flex encoder. The net effect is a live ingest operation that scales across locations and time zones without adding operational risk or headcount, turning content acquisition from a bottleneck into a controlled, repeatable capability.

The updates significantly expand Dalet’s embedded AI capabilities, allowing organizations to automatically enrich media assets as they enter the production workflow.

Advanced vision models are embedded directly within the Dalet Flex infrastructure, enabling AI to process content where the media resides. As assets enter production, the platform can automatically generate descriptive metadata, identify objects, recognize emotional context and perform content moderation analysis without requiring media transfers to external AI services. This intelligence surfaces directly within Dalet Flex through timeline-based metadata and asset views, making content easier to understand, search and repurpose throughout its life cycle.

By automatically generating rich metadata during ingest, organizations can reduce manual logging while improving content discoverability, increasing the long-term value of growing media libraries and reducing manual data indexing efforts.

Enhancements to Dalet Cut introduce automated background blur for vertical video production, new subject-tracking blur capabilities to protect identities and sensitive information, improved text positioning and expanded image adjustment controls, including brightness and saturation. Editors can complete more finishing work directly within their production workflow while reducing the need for additional applications.

The release also streamlines content preparation for distribution. Updated workflow wizards simplify packaging processes, while new caption burn-in capabilities within Dalet Flex Stream Processing integrate accessibility and compliance tasks directly into automated delivery workflows. Together with expanded media format support, these enhancements accelerate the journey from acquisition to publication.

This release turns Dalia into an operational force multiplier across the media supply chain. Any workflow in a Flex environment can now be exposed to Dalia through simple configuration, with no custom development required, so teams can execute complex operations using natural language rather than specialized interface expertise.

Dalia automatically discovers any workflow present in the system, while Workflow Designer gives teams precise control over which workflows are exposed to Dalia. Once a workflow is surfaced, Dalia understands its structure and prompts the user for any variables required to run it, turning complex operational processes into a simple, guided conversation.

From media processing and metadata enrichment to packaging, review and content delivery, users can now initiate workflows in natural language, interacting with Dalet Flex more intuitively while sidestepping the complexity of traditional application interfaces.
